title: Gratitude: A Bible Study on Thanksgiving and Grace
subtitle: A five-session study on gratitude, grace, and the eucharistic heart.
summary:
This study is for anyone tired of gratitude taught as a life hack: a mood to manufacture, a journal you keep until the good feelings come. It's for people who want to know what thanks actually is and where it comes from. Its five sessions look at why Scripture names ingratitude as the first turn away from God rather than a small failing; at eucharisteo, the word for giving thanks, and the meal the church named after it; at gratitude tested in plenty and in want, with the ten lepers and the difference between thanks "in" all circumstances and thanks "for" them; at gratitude and grief held together; and at the ordinary practices that slowly form a grateful heart.

It's built so a busy small group or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer rather than in a performance of thankfulness.

One thing this study will never do is tell a grieving person to be grateful for the grave, or hand someone who is suffering a command to smile. Scripture asks for thanks in all circumstances, not for all of them. Gratitude in the Bible walks through grief rather than papering over it. Where there's real despair, the study keeps the way to help in plain view. Thanks was never a mood to fake. It's the recognition that a whole life is unearned, spoken to the One who gave it.
audience: Small groups, individuals, and anyone learning to live grateful

sessions.title: The Sin We Would Never Call a Sin
sessions.aim: To name ingratitude not as a mild failing or a matter of temperament but as the first turn of the human heart away from God, while refusing both the shallow positivity that fakes thanks and the entitlement that receives a whole life as owed.
sessions.summary:
You can sit at a full table on an ordinary Thursday, children talking over each other, food nobody went hungry to earn, and feel nothing. Not sadness. Just the flat blindness of someone who takes it all as owed. It's the one sin almost no one would call a sin.

Paul traces the human turn away from God in Romans 1, and we expect the first step to be murder or idolatry. It isn't. "They did not honor him as God or give thanks to him" (Romans 1:21). Ingratitude comes first, and the rest grows from it.

There's a fair objection: gratitude is a temperament, and calling its absence sin shames the depressed and the grieving. That concern is real, and the session guards it. But Paul isn't describing a mood. He's describing a posture toward life itself, whether it's received as a gift or held as a possession. Gratitude isn't the reward for a good life. It's the first honest look at an unearned one.

keyScripture.why: "For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (Romans 1:21). The refusal to give thanks isn't a minor lapse. It's where the human turn from God begins.

discussion.q: Think of a full table, or a good ordinary day, where you felt nothing in particular. Where in your life have you stopped seeing what's in front of you and started receiving it as your due?
discussion.behind: Start with the texture before the theology. The blindness isn't dramatic. It's the flat familiarity of the well-fed: the roof, the health, the people, all taken as the baseline. Help the room find the actual places they've stopped seeing. Keep it on honesty, not guilt.

discussion.q: Read Romans 1:18-25. Paul puts the refusal to give thanks near the front of the human turn from God, before the idolatry and the violence. Why do you think it comes first?
discussion.behind: Press on the surprise. We'd put murder first. Paul puts ingratitude near the root, because failing to honor and thank God is the heart deciding it is owed rather than given. Verse 25 shows where it goes next: worship transferred to created things. This is a diagnosis, not a lesson in manners.

discussion.q: Some people say gratitude is just temperament, and that calling ingratitude a sin shames the depressed and grieving. What's true in that, and what should we be careful not to lose?
discussion.behind: Protect the vulnerable early. Gratitude does get turned into cruelty, the command to smile handed to the suffering. Make sure no one hears this session as a demand for cheerfulness. What Paul names is entitlement, not sorrow, and they aren't the same thing.

discussion.q: What's the difference between feeling down and being entitled? Which has more grip on you?
discussion.behind: Draw the line the last question protected. Sadness is honest about a real loss. Entitlement is a settled assumption that the good is owed, which no circumstance produces and none cures. Help each person find the entitlement under their complaints without confusing it with real grief. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 4:7. Where have you been keeping a quiet invoice against God for a life you assumed you were owed?
discussion.behind: "What do you have that you did not receive?" The invoice is the running account of what we think we were promised and didn't get. You aren't hunting for shame. You want each person, you included, inside the question, because thanks means little until you've seen the entitlement it replaces. Name your own first.

objections.objection: Gratitude is a personality trait. Some people are naturally optimistic and some aren't, and calling ingratitude a sin piles guilt on people who are already struggling, especially the depressed and the anxious, who can't just decide to feel thankful.
objections.response: There's a real cruelty to guard against here. Gratitude does get turned into a grinning positivity that tells a suffering person to count her blessings and buries her pain, and any teaching that uses thanks as a weapon against the depressed has misread the text. Depression isn't the sin Paul names, and no one should leave this session thinking their sorrow is a moral failure. But the objection confuses a mood with a posture. Paul isn't describing emotional weather some people get and others don't. He's describing the most basic stance a heart can take toward life, whether it receives it as a gift or seizes it as a possession. A naturally sunny person can be deeply entitled. A person fighting depression can be, underneath the pain, deeply grateful. The sin isn't the absence of a feeling. It's the refusal to honor the Giver.

objections.objection: Why would God need my thanks anyway? A God who demands gratitude from creatures he made sounds insecure, like a king who needs flattery to feel important.
objections.response: God doesn't need your gratitude the way an insecure king needs flattery, and Scripture never presents him as diminished when it's withheld. That's the point the objection misses. Thanks doesn't complete God. It's the one stance in which a creature sees things as they are: received, not owned. To refuse thanks isn't to injure God. It's to misdescribe your own life, to stand inside a breath you didn't earn and call it yours by right. The command to give thanks isn't God fishing for compliments. It's God calling you out of the illusion that you're the source of your own life.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the one good thing in your life you've completely stopped seeing, the gift so familiar it's become invisible, and when did you last thank God for it by name?
sessions.practice: This week, at one meal a day, stop before you eat and actually look at the food: where it came from, the hands and the ground and the God behind them. Name one thing you've been taking as owed, and say thank you out loud to the Giver. Don't perform it for anyone. Write down what happens in you the first time you really see something you'd stopped seeing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've sat at full tables and felt nothing, taken the breath and the roof and the people as things owed to us, and kept a quiet invoice against you. Forgive a blindness we'd never have called a sin, and the entitlement hiding under our complaints. Open our eyes to see that we made none of it, earned none of it, scheduled not one sunrise, and that all of it, down to this next breath, comes from your hand. Teach us to honor you as God and give you thanks, not because you need it but because we need to see truly. And where there's real grief in this room, let no one hear a demand to smile, only an invitation to see. Amen.
reflection: Where have I gone blind to a gift so familiar that I now receive it as the baseline?
Is what grips me honest sorrow over a real loss, or entitlement dressed up as disappointment?
If ingratitude is the first turn away from God, where has my own turning begun, and what would it look like to turn back with thanks?
sessions.teaching:
Picture a full table on an ordinary Thursday. Children are talking over each other, there's food nobody went hungry to earn, and the person at the head of it feels nothing. Not sadness. Just the flatness of someone who has stopped seeing what's in front of him and takes the whole thing as owed. It's the one sin most of us would never call a sin. It doesn't look like sin at all, and it hides so well inside a comfortable, respectable life that we can carry it for decades without confessing it.

Paul does something in Romans 1 that should stop us. He's tracing the human race's turn away from God, the whole slide, and we'd expect the first step to be murder or idolatry or violence. It isn't. He says that people knew God, and then he names the hinge: "they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (Romans 1:21). A few verses later comes the rest: they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). Ingratitude isn't a minor failing near the bottom of a list. It's near the root, the small refusal that darkens what follows. A heart that won't receive its life as a gift doesn't stay empty. It hands its worship to something else.

A thoughtful person will push back, and the objection deserves a fair hearing. Gratitude, it says, is temperament. Some people are built glass-half-full and some aren't, and calling ingratitude sin shames the depressed and the anxious and the grieving for a chemistry they didn't choose. There's real truth in that and a real cruelty to avoid. Gratitude does get counterfeited into the grinning positivity that tells a suffering woman to count her blessings and buries her pain under a command to smile. Any teaching that uses this text as a club against the sorrowing has misread it. I want that said clearly, because the rest of this means nothing if a grieving person hears it as an accusation.

But Paul isn't describing a mood. He's describing a posture toward life, the most basic one there is: whether you receive your life as a gift or seize it as a possession. That posture isn't handed out by temperament. The cheerful and the melancholy both choose it. A sunny man can be deeply entitled. A woman fighting depression can be, beneath the ache, profoundly grateful. The ungrateful heart in Romans 1 isn't sad. It's entitled, and entitlement is a kind of blindness. It has looked at a world it didn't make, a breath it didn't earn, and a sunrise it didn't schedule, and concluded that all of it is simply owed.

This is where I have to stand inside the diagnosis. Most of us run on an assumption we never examine: that the universe is in our debt, that a decent life is the baseline we're entitled to. So we live in a low, steady disappointment that the payments keep coming up short. Paul puts the question that ends the argument: "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). And none of us leaves the blindness behind as cleanly as we'd like. It comes back at the full table, in the health we assume and the people we take for granted, every time we receive a gift as if it were a wage.

That's why the objection about mood misses the weight of it. The problem was never that we didn't feel cheerful. The problem is that we couldn't see. We stood inside a life full of gifts and called it ours by right.

What breaks the blindness is simple and hard. Gratitude isn't the reward for a good life. It's the first honest look at an unearned one. It's the moment the recipient stops pretending to be the source, when you see that you didn't make the world and can't keep your heart beating for the next ten seconds, and that every good thing in your hands came from somewhere else. James says, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights" (James 1:17). That seeing isn't a mood. It's the truth about who you are: a creature and not the Creator, a guest and not the owner. Recovering thanks is recovering reality, and it starts when you admit you didn't earn the breath you've been using to complain.

scriptureStudy.note: "They did not honor him as God or give thanks to him." Paul puts the refusal of thanks at the head of the human turn from God. Gratitude isn't optional decoration; it's the fitting response of a creature, and its absence is where the darkening begins.

"They exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." The ungrateful heart doesn't stay empty. It moves its worship, which is why ingratitude and idolatry sit side by side.

"Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth." The entitled heart says "my hand did this," and the cure is remembering who gave it.

"This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" The rich man calls his barns and years his own, and God calls it folly. A life you can't keep for one more night was always a loan.
"What do you have that you did not receive?" One question closes off entitlement. Everything you have was given, and the fitting response to a received life is thanks, not boasting.

"Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." The good in your life isn't a neutral baseline. It comes down from a Giver, and the right response goes back up to him.
"Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." The command is against forgetting. The commonest ingratitude isn't defiance but slow amnesia.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, compare the older Christian reading of ingratitude with the newer therapeutic one. For most of Christian history gratitude was treated as a basic orientation of the soul rather than a pleasant emotion, and its absence as close to the root of sin. Augustine's Confessions tells the story of a restless heart that looked in created things for what only God could give. Luther, lecturing on Romans in 1515 and 1516, described sin as the heart curved in on itself. Set that beside the modern view of gratitude as a wellness practice that lowers stress.

The research is worth granting. Since Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough's studies in 2003, many researchers have found that regularly counting blessings is linked to greater well-being. That's true as far as it goes. But it can measure the benefits of thanks without answering the question that matters most: thanks to whom? Chesterton wrote in Orthodoxy that he felt grateful "though I hardly knew to whom," and he took that as a clue pointing toward God. Ask the group whether thanks aimed at luck or at no one can bear its own emptiness. Then take the harder turn: if ingratitude is near the root of sin, a comfortable life is more exposed to it, not less, because comfort dulls the eyes. The flatness people feel in the middle of plenty may be less a chemical accident than a spiritual symptom.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is kind, generous, and cheerful, and when the session names ingratitude as a root sin she's puzzled. She doesn't feel ungrateful. She feels lucky, she says warmly, and she's always tried to have a good attitude.

Honor her before you press. Her cheerfulness is real and it's a grace; a sour cynicism is no closer to gratitude than a shallow optimism. But notice the word "lucky." To feel fortunate is to register that good things have come your way. To stop there is to thank no one. The danger isn't that she's bitter; she plainly isn't. It's that her gratitude has never found its way to a Giver.

Don't let her hear this as an attack on her nature. Ask her gently whom she's been thanking all these years, and let Chesterton's line, "I felt grateful, though I hardly knew to whom," sit in the room. Then ask the group where their own thanks has had no one on the other end.

sessions.title: Eucharisteo, and the Meal Named for Thanks
sessions.aim: To recover thanksgiving as the shape of the whole Christian life and not a technique for feeling better, by sitting with what Jesus did over the bread on the night he was betrayed and the meal the church named after it.
sessions.summary:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread, "and when he had given thanks, he broke it" (Luke 22:19). The verb is eucharisteo, and early Christians named their central meal from it: the Eucharist, thanksgiving. Why would the church name its holiest act with the ordinary word for saying thank you? Because gratitude isn't one Christian activity among many. It's the shape of the whole.

Ann Voskamp has drawn attention to a family of Greek words, charis (grace), eucharisteo (giving thanks), and chara (joy), that share a root: grace received, thanks given, joy following. That's a real gift. But gratitude can also turn into a technique, a counting done to manage a mood with the Giver left out.

What guards against that is when Jesus gave thanks: over his own body about to be broken, with Judas already gone. Christian thanks can be spoken facing the cross, because it rests on who God is. A list of blessings with no one to receive them is a ledger, not a Eucharist.

keyScripture.why: "And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you'" (Luke 22:19). Jesus gave thanks over the bread that was his own body about to be broken, and the church named its central meal for that thanksgiving.

discussion.q: The church named its central act of worship the Eucharist, thanksgiving, after Jesus gave thanks over the bread. What does it tell you that the holiest thing the church does is named for thanks?
discussion.behind: Start with the surprise. We might expect the meal to be named for sacrifice or remembrance. It's named for thanks. Let that reframe what people thought gratitude was: not a courtesy at the edges but something at the center of worship.

discussion.q: Grace received, thanks given, joy following. Where in that chain do you tend to get stuck?
discussion.behind: Let people find their own break. Some receive grace and never give thanks. Some give thanks mechanically and never arrive at joy. Some chase joy directly and skip the grace and the thanks. Help the room see the order: joy comes downstream of thanks, and thanks downstream of grace.

discussion.q: Have you ever practiced gratitude as a method for feeling better rather than as worship? What was the difference?
discussion.behind: Counting gifts can be good. The line is the Giver. Thanks aimed at God is worship; thanks aimed at your own mood is management, and the same habit can be either. Help people look at their own habits without shaming the practice. Go first.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 11:23-24. Paul keeps the timing: "on the night when he was betrayed." What changes about gratitude when you see that Jesus gave thanks facing the cross?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. That thanks wasn't for pleasant circumstances; it was spoken into betrayal and toward death, resting on the Father and not the situation. Help the room see that this frees gratitude from circumstance without denying the horror.

discussion.q: Where has your own gratitude become a ledger you keep to reassure yourself, rather than thanks you give to someone?
discussion.behind: The ledger is thanks turned inward, a list with no one on the other end. The Eucharist is thanks handed back to God. Let people notice which they've been doing, and let the difference speak for itself.

objections.objection: This is just the gratitude practice the wellness apps sell, keeping a list of things you're thankful for, dressed up in Greek and religion. It works because listing good things lifts your mood, not because of any God behind it.
objections.response: The overlap is real and worth admitting. Naming gifts does lift the mood, and a Christian counting his blessings and someone keeping a gratitude list can look nearly identical from the outside. But the objection assumes the lift is the point, that gratitude is justified by what it does for you. That's the reduction eucharisteo resists. Christian thanksgiving is worship aimed at a Giver, and the joy it brings is a byproduct, not the goal. Make the mood the point and you've left the Giver out and kept the technique. The two can look the same for a while. They part ways when life turns dark, because a technique aimed at feeling good has nothing to say to a cross, and thanks aimed at God can be spoken from one, as Jesus showed on the night he was betrayed.

objections.objection: How is anyone supposed to give thanks like Jesus did over his own coming death? Holding up the Son of God as the model just makes ordinary people feel like failures when they can't produce gratitude in a crisis.
objections.response: That concern protects something true: we should never lay a burden on the suffering they can't carry. No one produces thanks in a crisis by willpower, and anyone who tells you to summon gratitude over a grave is asking for a performance. But the objection assumes gratitude is something you generate from your own reserves, and that isn't where it comes from. Jesus didn't give thanks in the upper room by mustering a feeling. He gave thanks because he knew and trusted the Father and could hand even what was coming back to a hand he knew was good. That kind of thanks isn't a heroic emotion. It's a relationship spoken aloud. You don't climb up to it. You grow into it, slowly, as you come to know the God you're thanking, and it's never a demand laid on your worst day.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you give thanks, is there someone on the other end of it, or has your gratitude become a list you keep to reassure yourself?
sessions.practice: This week, take one hard or ordinary thing you'd never think to thank God for. Don't pretend it's good. Hand it back to him the way Jesus handed back the bread, and say something like, "I don't understand this, but I give it to you, and I thank you that you're still good in it." And once this week, take the Lord's Supper, or simply eat a meal, slowly, as thanks given to God rather than a list kept for yourself. Write down what it's like to aim your thanks at a Person instead of a page.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, on the night you were betrayed you took bread and gave thanks, over your own body about to be broken, and your church named its holiest meal for that thanksgiving. Teach us thanks that isn't a technique for our own comfort but worship given to you: grace received, given back, and turning somehow into joy. Forgive the ledgers we've kept, the lists we made to manage our moods with your name left out. We can't climb up to the gratitude you showed at that table. Grow it in us slowly, as we come to know the Father you trusted, until we can hand even the hard bread back to a hand we've learned is good. Amen.
reflection: Where do I break the chain from grace received to thanks given to joy?
Has my gratitude become a technique aimed at my own mood rather than worship given to God?
What hard thing have I never brought to God with thanks, not thanking him for it but handing it back to him in it?
sessions.teaching:
The deepest thing about Christian gratitude is hidden in a single word and a meal. On the night he was betrayed, in the upper room, with the betrayer at the table and the cross a few hours away, Jesus took bread. Luke records what he did next with a verb the church never let go of: "when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them" (Luke 22:19). The word is eucharisteo. Within a few generations Christians were calling the meal itself the eucharist, the thanksgiving. Around AD 150 Justin Martyr wrote that this food "is called among us" by that name.

Why would the church name its holiest act with the ordinary word for saying thank you? Because gratitude isn't one Christian activity among many, one discipline on a list. It's the shape of the whole thing. Ann Voskamp, whose book many in the room may know, points to a family of Greek words. Charis is grace. Eucharisteo, giving thanks, is built on it. Chara, joy, grows from the same root. So the Christian life moves in an order: grace received, thanks given, joy following. Grace comes first. Thanks is the receiving spoken back. Joy is what happens in a heart that has learned to do the first two. That's a real recovery, and I'm grateful for it.

But it needs a caution. The practice she's known for, naming a thousand gifts, can go hollow if you aren't watching. Gratitude can quietly become a technique, a counting done to manage your own mood, with the Giver left out. The moment the counting is aimed at your feelings instead of at God, you've kept the practice and lost the point. You're left with a ledger, not a Eucharist.

What keeps Christian thanks from collapsing into a wellness routine is the timing. Jesus didn't give thanks at a feast in a season of ease. He gave thanks over bread that was his own body about to be broken. Paul keeps the timing on purpose: "the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it" (1 Corinthians 11:23-24). So Christian gratitude isn't, at root, thanks for good circumstances. It's thanks that can be spoken facing the cross, because it rests on something the circumstances can't reach, the character of a Father the Son knew to be good as the darkness closed in.

That's the difference between the Christian thing and the technique. A technique aimed at your mood has nothing to say to a grave. It works while life cooperates and goes quiet when it doesn't. Thanks that rests on who God is can be spoken from a prison, and it has been. In 1943, writing from a cell in Berlin, Dietrich Bonhoeffer told his family that in ordinary life we hardly realize how much more we receive than we give, and that it's only with gratitude that life becomes rich. He was hanged in April 1945. He wasn't managing his mood. He was telling the truth from a place where every circumstance had failed, and he could do it because his thanks was aimed past the walls.

Most of us know the ledger better than we'd like to admit. I know I do. We count the gifts dutifully, the way you'd take a vitamin, hoping it'll lift the gray, and we reach the bottom of the page having thanked no one. Counting without the Giver isn't thanksgiving. It's bookkeeping.

Thanksgiving isn't a method for producing joy, something you run to get a result. It's where joy is found, because it's grace seen and named and handed back up to the God who gave it. Joy isn't a payoff waiting on the far side of the practice. It's what thanks becomes in a heart that means it, when the receiving and the returning complete the circle. Paul says, "whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him" (Colossians 3:17). The church named its meal for thanksgiving because the whole Christian life is pressed into it: grace taken in the hand, thanks spoken over it, and the broken body given for the life of the world.

scriptureStudy.note: "When he had given thanks, he broke it." The verb is eucharisteo, and the church's name for its central meal grew from it. The deepest act of Christian worship is, at root, thanks over bread that was a body about to be broken.

"The Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it." Paul keeps the thanks and the betrayal in one sentence, so Christian gratitude is marked forever as something that can be spoken in the dark.

"Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him." Thanksgiving isn't a slot in the day but the manner in which everything is meant to be done.
"Rooted and built up in him and established in the faith... abounding in thanksgiving." Abounding thanks is a mark of maturity. A life growing in Christ grows more grateful, not less.

"What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD." The psalmist answers the question of how to repay God with a cup lifted in thanks.

"For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer." Thanksgiving is how the good creation is rightly received.
"Giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." Thanks as the constant of a Christian life, offered through Christ to the Father.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the history of the word and the meal. The Didache, an early Christian manual, already gives prayers "concerning the eucharist," and Justin Martyr, around AD 150, describes the Sunday gathering at bread and cup and says the food is called eucharist. The church didn't name its meal for guilt or duty, but for thanksgiving. Ask the group how far that is from the anxious or transactional ways the Supper is sometimes approached now.

Then hold the gift and the caution in Voskamp's work together: the real insight that grace, thanks, and joy belong together, and the risk that gratitude becomes a feeling to cultivate rather than a Giver to worship. Bring Bonhoeffer's prison letters in as the test. He wrote of gratitude not as the fruit of good fortune but as what makes life rich even in loss. The uncomfortable question for the group is whether their thanks rests on circumstance or on God, and whether it could survive a prison cell.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group has started a gratitude journal his counselor recommended. He says it's helped his anxiety, and he gets a little defensive when the session separates technique from worship, because the technique is working.

Affirm before you deepen. His anxiety is lower, and that's a good gift; say so plainly. The session isn't against counting gifts. It's against counting them at no one. The question to put to him gently is who he's writing the list for. If it's a ledger aimed at his own mood, it will help until the day his circumstances collapse, and then it may have little to say. If each entry becomes thanks handed up to a God he's coming to trust, it has something to hold when the anxiety comes back.

Don't let him hear this as a dismissal of what has helped. Ask the group whether their own thanks has someone to land on when the good circumstances don't.

sessions.title: In All Circumstances, Not For Them
sessions.aim: To recover a gratitude that survives both plenty and want, by seeing how comfort quietly forgets God and how Scripture commands thanks in every circumstance without ever asking anyone to thank God for evil.
sessions.summary:
Gratitude dies in two places you'd least expect: the full life and the emptied one. Ten lepers are healed, and only one comes back to give thanks. "Where are the nine?" Jesus asks (Luke 17:17). Nine men received the gift and kept walking. Plenty forgets, and Deuteronomy warned Israel that when they were full they would forget the Lord.

At the other end, Paul writes, "give thanks in all circumstances" (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and the word that matters is "in." Paul doesn't say thank God for all circumstances. Anyone who hears the verse as a command to be grateful for the cancer, the abuse, or the grave is right to recoil, because thanking God for evil would be a lie that wounds the sufferer again. Thanks in all circumstances reaches through the circumstance to the God who is still good in it.

Habakkuk stands before a ruined harvest and says, "yet I will rejoice in the LORD." The one leper who returned wasn't grateful because his situation was better than the others'. He saw the One behind the gift.

keyScripture.why: "Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Thanks offered in every situation, reaching through it to the Giver. The word is "in," not "for," so the verse never asks anyone to be grateful for evil.

discussion.q: Read Luke 17:11-19. Ten were healed and one came back. When things are going well in your life, what happens to your gratitude? Where have you been one of the nine?
discussion.behind: Start with the danger of the full life; a comfortable room is more at risk here than in want. The nine weren't villains. They were healed, glad, and busy, and they forgot. Help the room see that fullness tends to dull gratitude rather than sharpen it.

discussion.q: Read Deuteronomy 8:11-14. Which comforts in your life have gone so familiar that you've stopped seeing the Giver behind them?
discussion.behind: The warning isn't against plenty but against the forgetting plenty produces. Help people name specific comforts that have gone invisible, and steer them away from feeling guilty for having good things. The problem is the forgetting, not the fullness.

discussion.q: Paul says "give thanks in all circumstances," not "for" all circumstances. Why does that one word matter so much? Have you seen the verse misused?
discussion.behind: This is the turning point of the session, and it protects the suffering. The misreading makes the verse a command to be grateful for evil, which is a lie and a cruelty. Make sure no one leaves thinking Scripture asks them to thank God for their worst wound.

discussion.q: Read Habakkuk 3:17-18. What's the difference between thanking God in an empty season and pretending the emptiness is full?
discussion.behind: Habakkuk doesn't deny the ruin. He names it, the fig tree, the vine, the olive, the flock, and then reaches past it to God. Biblical thanks in want isn't positivity. It finds God in the dark while telling the truth about the dark.

discussion.q: Which is more your habit: forgetting God in plenty, or pretending to be grateful in pain?
discussion.behind: Some lose gratitude by being comfortable, some by faking it in grief. Both miss true thanks. Answer first. Let the one leper who came back stand as the picture of thanks that neither forgets nor pretends.

objections.objection: "Give thanks in all circumstances" is a cruel thing to say to someone whose child died, or who was abused, or who is dying. Telling suffering people to be grateful for what happened to them is the kind of religion that wounds the broken again.
objections.response: Agree with the concern first, because the cruelty it names is real and common. Telling a grieving parent to be grateful for their child's death, or a survivor to thank God for abuse, isn't faith. It's a lie, and it drives the knife deeper. But read the verse again slowly, because that cruelty rests on a misquotation. Paul didn't write "thank God for all circumstances." He wrote "give thanks in all circumstances." Even inside the worst thing that has happened to you, there remains a God who is good, who didn't author the evil and won't waste it, and to whom you can still turn. Thanks in that sense isn't gratitude for the wound. It's a hand reaching through the wound to find his. You're never asked to call the evil good. You're invited, when you're able and not a moment before, to find that he's still there, and to thank him for that.

objections.objection: If God is in control and I'm supposed to thank him in everything, then he's behind the bad things too, and thanking him in the middle of them makes him the author of my suffering. I'd rather be honest than grateful to a God like that.
objections.response: This asks an old and real question about God and evil that one session can't settle and shouldn't pretend to. Scripture holds that God is sovereign, and it also insists that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). Holding those together is one of the hard things in the faith. But thanking God in your suffering doesn't require believing he manufactured it. The leper didn't thank Jesus for his leprosy; he thanked him for the mercy that met him in it. Habakkuk didn't thank God for the failed harvest; he rejoiced in the God who remained when it failed. Thanks in all circumstances isn't a judgment that the circumstances are good. It's a refusal to let even the worst thing cut you off from the God who is with you in it. Truth about the dark and gratitude to God in it need each other.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: In the hardest thing you're carrying right now, can you find the difference between thanking God for it, which you may never be able to do, and thanking him that he's still with you in it?
sessions.practice: This week, in plenty, catch yourself once being one of the nine, receiving a good thing and walking on, and turn back like the one leper to thank the Giver by name. And in whatever is hard, practice the word "in": not thanking God for the thing, but reaching through it to say, "You're still here. You're still good. Thank you for that." Write down what you find when you stop trying to thank God for your pain and start thanking him in it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we're the nine more often than the one: healed, glad, and walking away, too full to remember the hand that filled us. Forgive the forgetting that comes with our comfort. And in the hard places, keep us from the lie that would thank you for evil, and teach us the thanks Habakkuk spoke before a ruined field, in all circumstances and not for them. Where anyone in this room is grieving, don't let them hear a command to be grateful for their wound. Let them hear that you're with them in it. You're still here. You're still good. We thank you for that. Amen.
reflection: Where has my comfort made me forget the Giver, so that I'm one of the nine who walked away healed?
Have I heard "give thanks in all circumstances" as a command to thank God for evil, and has that crushed me or hardened me?
In my hardest thing, what would it look like to stop straining to thank God for it and reach through it to the God who is still there?
sessions.teaching:
Gratitude dies in two places you'd least expect, at opposite ends of a life. It dies in the full life, and it dies in the emptied one, and Scripture has a word for both.

Start with fullness, because it's the more dangerous of the two and the one a comfortable room least suspects. Ten lepers meet Jesus on the road, men whose disease had cut them off from family, worship, and touch, and he heals all ten. Then "one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks" (Luke 17:15-16). Jesus asks, "Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?" (Luke 17:17). There's no villain among the nine. They were glad, healed, and hurrying home to the lives they'd lost, and they kept walking. The gift was so large it swallowed the Giver.

Deuteronomy saw this coming centuries earlier: "lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 8:12-14). Not rebel. Forget. Comfort works slowly, and the more good you have, the easier it is to stop seeing where it came from, until you're living in a life full of gifts and thanking no one.

The other end, the emptied life, needs more care, because this is where bad gratitude teaching does its damage. Paul writes, "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Some people hear that as a monstrous command: a mother told to thank God for her child's death, a survivor told to thank God for abuse. They're right to recoil. That would be a lie and a cruelty, religion that wounds the broken and calls it faith. So let me say it plainly. You're never asked to thank God for evil.

Read what Paul actually wrote. Not "for all circumstances" but "in all circumstances." The small Greek phrase, en panti, means in everything, in the middle of whatever comes. To thank God for evil would be to call darkness light. To thank God in the evil is to reach through the darkness and find that his hand is still there, that he didn't author the wound and won't waste it, and that he's still good here. Thanking him for that is the truest thing a sufferer can say without lying.

Habakkuk shows the shape of it. Facing ruin, he names it without flinching: "Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:17-18). He doesn't pretend the fig tree bloomed. He lists the losses, all of them, and then reaches past them to the God who remains when the harvest fails. That isn't positivity. It finds the Giver in the dark.

I've failed at both ends, and I suspect you have too. I've been one of the nine, receiving a hundred mercies a day without a backward glance. And in hard seasons I've gotten the word wrong the other way, either unable to thank God at all because I thought I was being asked to thank him for the hardness, or forcing out a gratitude for something that was simply evil and calling the forcing faith.

The leper who came back holds the cure for both. Look at why he returned. It wasn't that his situation was better than the others'. All ten were healed. What set him apart was that he "saw that he was healed" and turned from the cleansing to the One who cleansed him. That seeing is thanks that holds at both ends of a life. It doesn't rest on fullness that can vanish or emptiness that can crush. It rests on a Person who is good in the full house and good in the ruined field. As the psalm says, "Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever" (Psalm 107:1). Thanks in all circumstances isn't a feeling about your circumstances. It's a turning toward the God who is in all of them.

scriptureStudy.note: "One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks." The one who returned is marked by seeing. He turned from the healing to the Healer.

"Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?" It was the outsider, a Samaritan, who came back, a warning that religious familiarity can dull gratitude.
"Take care lest you forget the LORD your God... lest, when you have eaten and are full... your heart be lifted up, and you forget." The danger is forgetting, and the trigger is plenty, not scarcity.
"Give thanks in all circumstances." In, not for: thanks offered within every situation and reaching through it to God, never a command to be grateful for evil.
"Though the fig tree should not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD." Habakkuk names the ruin in full before he reaches past it. Thanks in want doesn't deny the loss.

"Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God." Thanksgiving is set against anxiety, offered in everything, the good and the fearful alike.

"Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever." The ground of thanks is God's character, not our circumstances, which is why thanks can hold when circumstances don't.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, stay with the difference between "in" and "for." In 1 Thessalonians 5:18 Paul writes en panti, "in everything." Compare Ephesians 5:20, "giving thanks always and for everything," which sounds harder. Don't flatten either verse. Even the "for everything" is offered "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ," in the confidence of Romans 8:28 that God "works all things together for good" for those who love him. That's a promise about God's power to redeem what he didn't author, not a claim that evil is good. Ask the group how they'd explain the difference to someone in fresh grief.

Then look at plenty. Psychologists describe "hedonic adaptation," our tendency to get used to good things quickly until we no longer notice them. It confirms the warning of Deuteronomy 8 that fullness breeds forgetting, though it names the mechanism without supplying the cure, which isn't a technique but deliberately remembering the Giver. The same passage frees the grieving from a false burden and wakes the comfortable from a real sleep.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group lost her husband a year ago. When the session reaches "give thanks in all circumstances," she goes quiet, then says, with some anger, that people at church told her to be grateful for what God was teaching her through his death. She can't do it, and it has nearly wrecked her faith.

Side with her against the bad teaching before you say anything else. She isn't failing. She was handed a misreading of Scripture, and her recoil is closer to truthfulness than to weak faith. Tell her so, and grieve with her that the church wounded her this way.

Only when she's ready, show her the word "in." Scripture never asked her to thank God for her husband's death. It invites something different: thanks, whenever and if ever she can, to the God who has been with her in the dark of losing him. Don't rush her. Grief this fresh may need more than a study, so make sure she knows where real help is. Then ask the group where they've been handed a burden Scripture never laid on them.

memoryVerse.text: Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

sessions.title: Lament and Thanks Are Not Enemies
sessions.aim: To hold gratitude and grief together rather than setting them against each other, refusing both the false choice that says you must feel better before you can give thanks and the false comfort that buries grief under forced gratitude.
sessions.summary:
The cruelest lie about gratitude is that it cancels grief: that you have to feel better before you're allowed to give thanks. That shuts the grieving out of thanksgiving until they've finished mourning, which for the deepest losses is never. The Psalms won't allow it. The same book holds Psalm 100, "Enter his gates with thanksgiving," and Psalm 13, "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?"

Lament without thanks can harden into despair. Thanks without lament shrinks into a lie. Job, told he's lost everything, says, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21), and then laments for chapters. Lamentations, written from a ruined city, reaches "his mercies never come to an end."

The objection that this is spiritual bypassing, tying a bow on a wound, names a real abuse. But biblical thanks doesn't skip grief. It walks through it. Lament isn't the opposite of thanks. It's thanks that won't lie about the wound, offered to the God who wept at a grave he was about to open.

keyScripture.why: "The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:22-23). Spoken from the ashes of Jerusalem, it holds thanks and grief in the same breath. Gratitude doesn't deny the ruin; it reaches through it to the God who remains.

discussion.q: Where have you believed you had to feel better before you were allowed to be grateful?
discussion.behind: Go carefully; some in the room are grieving now. The lie shuts the sorrowing out of thanks until they stop hurting, so they conclude gratitude isn't for them. Make it safe to be grieving and present without performing a recovery no one has made.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 100 and Psalm 13 side by side. What does it mean that Scripture puts thanks and lament in the same book of worship?
discussion.behind: A church that sings only the thanks and never the lament has cut its songbook in half and left the grieving with nothing to sing. Help the room see lament as a form of faith, not a failure of it. Notice too that Psalm 13 ends in trust (13:5-6) without the circumstance changing.

discussion.q: Read Job 1:20-22. How does Job hold the giving and the taking together without pretending the grief away?
discussion.behind: Handle this with reverence. Job isn't calm or in denial; the rest of the book is raw lament. This first response holds gift and loss in the same sentence. Blessing God in loss isn't the same as feeling fine about it. Note Job 42:7, where God says Job spoke rightly and the tidy friends didn't.

discussion.q: Where has forced gratitude been used on you, or by you, to hurry past a grief that needed to be felt?
discussion.behind: This names a real abuse. Forced gratitude that rushes past grief often manages other people's discomfort rather than caring for the sufferer. Help the room tell the difference between false comfort that buries grief and true thanks that walks through it. No one should be shamed for having done either.

discussion.q: If lament is a form of faith rather than a failure of it, what could you bring to God that you've been keeping back?
discussion.behind: Close on the God who receives both the thanks and the "how long." People don't have to choose between truth about their pain and gratitude toward God. Jesus wept at a grave. End with that weight; don't resolve it.

objections.objection: This is spiritual bypassing with better packaging. Telling grieving people they can be grateful and sad at the same time still pushes gratitude on them before they're ready. It ties a bow on a wound that needs to bleed for a while.
objections.response: Spiritual bypassing is real, and this session is trying hard not to do it. Forced gratitude that hurries a grieving person past their pain usually serves the comfortable person's discomfort, not the sufferer. If this teaching said "cheer up and count your blessings," the objection would be exactly right. But bypassing skips the grief, and what Scripture models doesn't skip it. It walks through it, and it never asks the sorrowing to feel grateful on a schedule. Lament isn't the small print under gratitude; it's a large part of the songbook. The wound is allowed to bleed, as long as it bleeds, before a God who can bear it. And if somewhere in the middle a thanks rises, not for the wound but toward the God who hasn't left, that isn't a denial of grief. It's grief refusing to conclude that God is gone.

objections.objection: If I really trusted God, I wouldn't need to lament. Complaining to God about my suffering seems like the opposite of gratitude, like accusing him. Shouldn't a grateful believer just accept what comes?
objections.response: This needs correcting in the other direction. The idea that a faithful person never laments, only accepts and gives thanks, isn't in the Bible. It's stoicism in Christian clothes. About a third of the Psalms are laments, and God put them in his people's songbook, which means he invites the crying out and receives it. You only lament to someone you believe is listening and could act. The person who has stopped lamenting has often grown more resigned, not more faithful. Job complained for chapters, and at the end God said the friends who defended him with tidy answers had "not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). Don't mistake suppressed grief for gratitude. The most grateful people in Scripture were also the most honest about their pain.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What grief have you kept out of your prayers because you thought a grateful person wasn't allowed to bring it, and what would it be like to hand God the thanks and the wound in the same breath?
sessions.practice: This week, pray one prayer that holds both, the way Job and the Psalms do. Tell God plainly what hurts, without softening it. In the same prayer, name one thing you can still thank him for, not to cancel the grief but to sit beside it. Don't force the two to resolve. Write down what it was like to be honest about a wound and grateful to God at the same time.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave us a songbook with "enter his gates with thanksgiving" on one page and "how long, O LORD" on another, and you meant both to live in the same heart. Forgive us for believing we had to feel better before we could come to you, and for the times we forced gratitude on ourselves or others to skip a wound that needed to bleed. Teach us the thanks that walks through grief instead of around it, the blessing Job spoke in his loss, the mercy Jeremiah's city found new every morning in its ashes. Where anyone here is grieving, don't let them hear that thanks is closed to them until the pain is gone. Meet them as your Son met Mary and Martha, weeping at the grave he was about to open. Amen.
reflection: Where have I believed I had to feel better before I could give thanks, and shut myself out of gratitude while I grieved?
Have I used gratitude, on myself or others, to skip a grief that needed to be felt?
What would it look like to bring God my lament and my thanks in the same prayer?
sessions.teaching:
The cruelest lie ever told about gratitude is that it cancels grief. It says, in a hundred gentle and destructive ways, that you have to feel better before you're allowed to give thanks, that gratitude and mourning can't share a room. So the grieving are quietly shut out of thanksgiving until they've finished grieving, which for the deepest losses never happens. The bereaved mother, the man whose marriage ended, the believer sitting with a diagnosis, all hear the same closed door: thanks is for the healed, come back when you're whole.

The Psalms won't allow it. Look at the songbook God gave his people. The same book that gives us "Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise" (Psalm 100:4) gives us, a few pages earlier, "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). Both are in the songbook. Both are prayers God authorized. He didn't put thanks in a book for the happy and lament in a book for the faithless. He put them side by side because they'd live side by side in the same heart, often on the same day. Psalm 13 itself turns, before it ends, to "But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation" (Psalm 13:5), and nothing in the psalm says the trouble has passed.

So lament and thanks aren't enemies. They need each other. Lament without thanks can harden over time into despair, a crying out that has decided no one is listening. Thanks without lament shrinks into a lie, a gratitude that can only be spoken by pretending the wounds aren't there, and it goes silent the moment life gets hard. Held together, they make a faith that can look at the whole of life, the gift and the grief, and still speak to God.

Watch Job. By the end of a single afternoon he has lost his wealth, his servants, and all ten of his children. He tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships: "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21). Don't read that as stoic calm. The same man spends most of the book in the rawest lament in Scripture, cursing the day he was born and demanding an answer from God. Job isn't fine. But in that first moment he holds the giving and the taking in one sentence, blessing God without denying the loss.

The objection here deserves a full hearing, because it guards something true. It calls all this spiritual bypassing, forcing a bow onto a wound that needs to bleed, and that abuse is everywhere. Bad gratitude teaching rushes the grieving toward a silver lining and ties a ribbon on a fresh grave. Often it's managing the comfortable person's discomfort by hurrying the sufferer along. Grant all of it. But the abuse skips the grief, and biblical thanks walks straight through it.

There's a whole book of the Bible for this. Lamentations is five chapters of grief written after Jerusalem's destruction, the temple burned and the people taken away. It holds nothing back. The poet describes being walled in, driven into darkness, his teeth ground on gravel (Lamentations 3:7, 2, 16). Then, in the middle of the book, he writes: "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:21-23). He doesn't deny the ruin. He's sitting in it, and from inside it he reaches for a mercy that's new every morning.

Bonhoeffer, writing from prison, said something like this too: that gratitude changes the pain of memory into a quieter joy. I don't take him to mean that gratitude erased what he'd lost. I take him to mean that thanks, brought to memories that ached, slowly changed them, giving the grief somewhere to rest.

So I won't hand anyone a thanks that skips their sorrow. That would be the very abuse the objection names. But I also won't tell a grieving person the door to thanks is locked until the pain is gone, because that's the first lie, and it leaves them nothing to sing. Lament isn't the opposite of thanks. It's thanks that refuses to lie about the wound, faith that can say to God, "This is unbearable," and "You're still good," in the same breath. And the God who receives both isn't standing at a safe distance demanding a cheerful face. At the grave of his friend, knowing he was minutes from raising him, "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). He gives us the tears and the thanks in the same person, at the same tomb.

scriptureStudy.note: "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Job holds gift and loss in one sentence, and the lament that follows shows this is worship, not stoicism.
"How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" God put this cry in the same songbook as the thanksgiving psalms. Lament is an authorized prayer, spoken to someone believed to be listening.

"But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me." The psalm that began with "how long" ends in thanks, not because the circumstance changed but because the psalmist reached back to God's character.

"Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall... But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope." The poet names the ruin and then reaches through it to mercies new every morning.
"Jesus wept." At Lazarus's grave, minutes before raising him, Jesus grieves. The God who receives our thanks also weeps at our graves.
"As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing." Paul describes sorrow and joy held together in the same life, not one giving way to the other.

"You have turned for me my mourning into dancing... that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent." The turn from mourning to thanks is God's work over time, not a switch the grieving person flips.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the theology of lament, which much of the modern church has lost, and whose loss makes forced gratitude possible. Walter Brueggemann, in The Message of the Psalms (1984), reads the Psalms as songs of orientation, disorientation, and new orientation, and he argued that a worship life that sings only the first kind can't tell the truth about suffering. Ask how much that describes your own church, where the songs may be relentlessly upbeat and the grieving have nothing to sing. Michael Card's A Sacred Sorrow makes a similar case for ordinary readers.

Counselors often say that grief that isn't named doesn't disappear but goes underground. Treat that as a finding to test, not swallow, and notice that it agrees with what the lament psalms modeled long ago, while the Psalms add the One the grief is spoken to. The hardest question for the group is whether their faith has room for lament, or whether they've absorbed a stoicism that treats complaint as unbelief, and whether recovering lament might be what makes their gratitude true enough to survive real loss.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group lost his job eight months ago and hasn't found another. He tells you he's stopped praying. He feels he has nothing to be thankful for, and he doesn't want to come to God as a complainer, so he's gone silent.

His instinct not to fake gratitude is right; honor it. But he's drawn the wrong conclusion, that the only alternative to fake thanks is silence. Show him the lament psalms, God's own invitation to bring the complaint, and show him that lament is a form of faith, spoken only to a God you believe is there. His silence can look like humility while it's really a slow drifting away.

Don't push him toward gratitude he can't feel. Push him back toward honest prayer of any kind: "how long," "this is unbearable," "where are you." Job's complaint was received. It's often on the far side of a real lament that real thanks rises. Ask the group what they've stopped saying to God because they thought he didn't want to hear it.
